title: Two Pairs of Half-Knit Stockings and a Hospital Run by Women
dek: In 1856 Elizabeth Blackwell and Marie Zakrzewska gave themselves a year to open a hospital run entirely by women; with Emily Blackwell they opened it on Bleecker Street in May 1857.

story.founder: Elizabeth Blackwell, Emily Blackwell and Marie Zakrzewska
story.company: New York Infirmary for Indigent Women and Children
story.event: Opening the first hospital in the United States run entirely by women physicians
story.summary: In 1856 Elizabeth Blackwell, who had run a small dispensary for poor women in New York since 1853, agreed with the newly qualified Marie Zakrzewska to open a small hospital within a year rather than wait for a large fund. With Emily Blackwell as surgeon and Zakrzewska as resident physician, the New York Infirmary for Indigent Women and Children opened at 64 Bleecker Street in May 1857 despite warnings that no one would rent to them or fund them; its beds filled within a month, and Emily Blackwell ran it for some forty years.
paragraphs: On the evening of 1 May 1856, by Marie Zakrzewska's account, she and Elizabeth Blackwell agreed that a hospital run by women would open in New York in exactly one year. Blackwell, the first woman to earn an American medical degree, had since 1853 run a dispensary for poor women in a single room near Tompkins Square, three afternoons a week. Zakrzewska, just qualified in Cleveland, woke next morning and noted that "the funds towards it are two pairs of half-knit babies' stockings."

They knew the obstacles. No hospital anywhere let women physicians practise or train. People they asked for help warned, the infirmary's 1864 report recorded, that no one would rent them a house, that the police would interfere, that their death certificates would not be recognised, and that they would never raise enough money. Blackwell had written to her sister Emily, then training in Europe, that "the medical solitude is really awful at times." Zakrzewska argued for opening a small hospital quickly instead of waiting for a large fund, and Blackwell agreed.

Helped by Quaker friends and the journalist Mary Booth's newspaper notices, they rented an old house at 64 Bleecker Street and ordered 24 iron bedsteads for $100: a dispensary downstairs, two wards of six beds, and a maternity floor. Emily, back from Europe, took charge of surgery; Zakrzewska became resident physician. In May 1857 the infirmary was formally opened at a public meeting where Henry Ward Beecher spoke. The patrons would not let either Blackwell speak, Zakrzewska recalled, for fear she would sound "like a Woman's Rights woman."

Within a month the beds were full and thirty or more outpatients came each day. Money stayed hard: Elizabeth wrote that the income rested mainly on their own efforts, with a bazaar every year for seven years, and the actress Fanny Kemble refused them a benefit reading because the doctors were women. When a mother died after childbirth, relatives gathered with pickaxes and shovels, shouting that the doctors were killing women; local policemen sent the crowd away. Emily Blackwell went on to run the infirmary for some forty years.

quote.text: The river has its boundaries, its banks, but is a river all banks? or are the banks the final facts about the river? Do not these obstructions themselves give its water an onward motion?
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore asks whether a river is all banks. The infirmary's banks were real: a rented house, borrowed male names, an opening at which its own doctors could not speak. Yet they also gave the work its channel, small and close to the poor, and it kept moving for decades.

reflection: Elizabeth Blackwell's phrase about medical solitude may sound familiar. Doing something new inside a profession can leave you without peers who see what you are attempting. What eased it for her was not a larger fund or a better argument, but people working beside her: a sister, a younger colleague, a few Quaker friends.

The warnings against the infirmary were mostly forecasts. Some came partly true; most did not. If you are carrying a list like that, it may help to sort it into facts and forecasts, and to think about who could stand beside you while you find out which is which.

cross_checks.claim: The New York Infirmary opened in May 1857 at 64 Bleecker Street, run by Elizabeth and Emily Blackwell with Marie Zakrzewska.
Elizabeth Blackwell had run a one-room dispensary for the poor, three afternoons a week, since 1853.
Emily Blackwell took charge of surgery and Zakrzewska was resident physician.
Henry Ward Beecher spoke at the opening meeting.
Emily Blackwell became the main force running the infirmary in the decades after Elizabeth and Zakrzewska left.

research_notes: Opening date: Elizabeth Blackwell's memoir says only that the infirmary was formally opened 'in the May of this year' (1857); Zakrzewska's memoir says 1 May 1857, the date the two had set a year earlier; EBSCO and the NYC LGBT Historic Sites Project give 12 May 1857. The story says 'in May 1857'. Speakers: Blackwell lists Beecher, Dr Elder of Philadelphia and the Rev. Dr Tyng; Zakrzewska lists Beecher, Elder and Dr Kissam; the story names only Beecher, whom both give. Emily's return: Blackwell dates it to 1856, while Zakrzewska says Emily had returned a few weeks before the opening; the story says only that Emily was back from Europe by the opening. Address: 64 Bleecker Street in the 1850s numbering, now 58 Bleecker Street (NYC LGBT Historic Sites). Name: the memoir and NLM say 'New York Infirmary for Women and Children'; EBSCO and the historic-sites project use 'New York Infirmary for Indigent Women and Children', which the slate also uses. Zakrzewska's memoir (edited by Agnes Vietor from her own writings, 1924) is the sole source for the 1 May 1856 agreement, the stockings, the bedsteads, the speaking ban and the crowd after a patient's death; these are attributed to her. The objections are quoted by Blackwell from the infirmary's 1864 Annual Report, so they are described as recorded later. Kemble's refusal is Blackwell's own account. Founders: the slate named the two sisters; Zakrzewska is added because both memoirs and NLM treat her as a founding physician. Forty years: NLM says Emily managed the infirmary for the next forty years. The Tagore passage concerns the problem of evil and imperfection in creation, applied here by analogy. No talQen mention. The repeat screen flagged editions on Ela Bhatt, Florence Nightingale, Robert Owen and Thérèse Izay as same-founder matches; they are different people and episodes, the screen let this edition through, and no field was reworded.
